titleEn: The Song of the Cid — The battle below Alcocer: Fáriz wounded, Galve routed (tiradas 35–39, lines 715–777)
part: Tiradas 35–39 · The battle below Alcocer: Fáriz wounded, Galve routed (lines 715–777)

sentences.t:
Enbraçan los escudos delant los coraçones,
abaxan las lanças abu[el]tas de los pendones,
enclinaron las caras de suso de los arzones,
ívanlos ferir de fuertes coraçones.
sentences.l:
They-grip the shields before the hearts,
they-lower the lances together-with the pennons,
they-bowed the faces above of the saddle-bows,
they-went-them to-strike with strong hearts.
sentences.i: They brace their shields before their hearts, they lower their lances, pennons and all, they bowed their faces over the saddle-bows, and went to strike them with stout hearts.
sentences.n: Tirada 35 (assonance ó-e) — the Çid's men charge to rescue Per Vermudoz (Pidal: Los del Cid acometen para socorrer a Pedro Vermúdez). The line-ends are ó-e (coraçones, pendones, arzones, colpes); the lines that end in a bare stressed ó (naçió, Criador, Campeador, Vermudoz, son) belong to the same tirada, sung with the paragogic -e (naçióe, Criadore) as in tirada 3. Pidal notes that this description of the knights' charge is repeated at vv. 3615–18. Enbraçan, 'they take on the arm' (the shield's straps go over the forearm, braço). abu[el]tas de = a bueltas de, the old phrase 'together with, along with' (literally 'at the turns of', bueltas from bolver); the el is Pidal's: the lances come down pennons and all. Perhaps the pennons are also wound about the shafts for the charge, but the phrase itself says only 'along with'. de suso de, 'above'; arzones, the high saddle-bows, over which the riders lean. ívanlos ferir, 'they went to strike them' (ivan + los; ferir = herir, f- for h-). The tenses slide from present to preterite to imperfect inside four lines, as they often do in the poem.

sentences.t:
A grandes vozes llama el que en buen ora na[çió]:
“¡feridlos, cavalleros, por amor de[l Criador]!
Yo so R[o]y Díaz, el Çid de Bivar Campeador!”
sentences.l:
With great voices calls he who in good hour was-born:
“strike-them, knights, for love of-the [Creator]!
I am R[o]y Díaz, the Çid of Bivar Campeador!”
sentences.i: With a great shout he calls out, he who was born in a good hour: “Strike them, knights, for the love of the Creator! I am Ruy Díaz, the Çid of Vivar, the Campeador!”
sentences.n: el que en buen ora na[çió], the 'born in a good hour' formula; the ending -çió is in italics in Pidal's print, i.e. supplied by him, as are the l of de[l] and the whole word [Criador]. feridlos, 'strike them' (imperative ferid + los). so = soy, 'I am'. R[o]y = Ruy (only the o is Pidal's). Pidal's note: it was the custom for the leader to shout his own name to put heart into his knights; he quotes Don Juan Manuel's Libro de los Estados, that the captain 'débese nombrar muchas veces a sí et a su apellido, et mandar que digan todos: feridlos, que vanse et vencidos son' ('must name himself and his war-cry many times, and order them all to shout: strike them, they are running and beaten'). The same cry comes again at v. 1140.

sentences.t: Todos fieren en el az do está Per Vermu[doz].
sentences.l: All strike in the line where is Per Vermu[doz].
sentences.i: All of them strike at the battle line where Per Vermudoz is.
sentences.n: The rescue: the whole company drives into the enemy line (az) that has swallowed the standard-bearer (v. 711). do = donde, 'where'. Per Vermu[doz]: the -doz is Pidal's, as before.

sentences.i: Three hundred lances they are, every one with its pennon; each man killed his Moor, each with a single blow; and as they wheel and charge back, as many more lie dead.
sentences.n: seños, 'one each' (the old distributive, modern sendos): Pidal glosses seños moros 'uno cada uno' and de seños colpes 'uno de cada golpe' — each knight one Moor, each Moor one blow. colpes = golpes. a la tornada, 'at the return': having ridden through the enemy line, the horsemen wheel and charge back through it; Pidal refers to his introduction for this manoeuvre. otros tantos, 'as many again'. [muertos], 'dead', is a whole word supplied by Pidal (printed in italics).

sentences.t:
Veriedes tantas lanças premer e alçar,
tanta adágara foradar e passar,
tanta loriga falssa[r e] desmanchar,
sentences.l:
You-would-see so-many lances press-down and raise,
so-much shield pierce and pass-through,
so-much hauberk break [and] unmail,
sentences.i: You would have seen so many lances lowered and raised, so many a shield pierced through, so many a hauberk split and its mail burst apart,
sentences.n: Tirada 36 (assonance á) — they shatter the enemy lines (Pidal: Destrozan las haces enemigas). The lines close on stressed á (alçar, passar, andar, logar, ya), and two close in á-e — sangre (729) and Yagüe (731): as in tirada 32, Old Spanish verse allows a paragogic -e after the stressed á, so these count as á-endings. Veriedes, 'you would see' (conditional of ver), the minstrel calling on his audience to picture the scene; it governs every infinitive down to v. 730. premer, 'to press down' (the lance couched for the thrust) and alçar, 'raise' (to strike again). adágara, 'leather shield' (Arabic, modern adarga); tanta adágara, 'so much shield' = so many a shield. foradar = horadar, 'to pierce' (f- for h-). falssa[r e]: Pidal's note on v. 713 explains falssar la loriga as breaking defensive armour; the r and the e 'and' are his. desmanchar: Pidal, 'desmallar', to break the mail or plates of the hauberk.

sentences.t:
tantos pendones blancos salir vermejos en sangre,
tantos buenos cavallos sin sos dueños andar.
sentences.l:
so-many pennons white come-out red in blood,
so-many good horses without their masters go.
sentences.i: so many white pennons coming out red with blood, so many good horses running without their riders.
sentences.n: The white pennons go into the bodies and come out (salir) red: vermejos = bermejos. sangre, an á-e ending in the á tirada (paragogic -e, see v. 726). sos dueños, 'their masters' (sos = sus). andar, 'to go about' — here loose and riderless.

sentences.t: Los moros llaman Mafómat e los cristianos santi Yagüe.
sentences.l: The Moors call Mafómat and the Christians saint Yagüe.
sentences.i: The Moors cry out on Muhammad, and the Christians on Saint James.
sentences.n: Mafómat, Muhammad; santi Yagüe, Saint James (Santiago), the war-cry of Christian Spain; Yagüe gives á-e in the á tirada. Pidal's note: the Moors could shout the name of Muhammad in battle as part of the usual invocation Bismi Allahi … 'in the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate; Muhammad is the envoy of God'; and the Christians, according to Archbishop Rodrigo of Toledo, used 'Dios ayuda y Santiago!' as their war-cry from the time of the Apostle's appearance at the battle of Clavijo.

sentences.t:
Ca[d]ien [por el campo] en un poco de logar
moros muertos mill e trezientos ya.
sentences.l:
There-were-falling [through the field] in a little of place
Moors dead thousand and three-hundred already.
sentences.i: Across the field, in a small space of ground, the Moors fell dead — a thousand three hundred of them by now.
sentences.n: Ca[d]ien = caían, 'were falling' (the d is Pidal's; the imperfect in -ié- as in avié, querié); [por el campo], 'across the field', a whole phrase supplied by Pidal (in italics). en un poco de logar, 'in a small space' (logar = lugar). ya, 'already', closes the tirada on a plain á. The numbers are epic, not a chronicle's.

sentences.t:
¡Quál lidia bien sobre exorado arzón
mio Çid Ruy Diaz el buen lidiador;
sentences.l:
How fights well upon gilded saddle-bow
my Çid Ruy Diaz the good fighter;
sentences.i: How well he fights upon his gilded saddle-bow, my Çid Ruy Díaz, the good fighter;
sentences.n: Tirada 37 (assonance ó) — the chief Christian knights named (Pidal: Mención de los principales caballeros cristianos). The line-ends are ó (arzón, lidiador, mandó, pro, Aragón, son); Salvadórez (739) is the ó tirada's ó-e. The exclamation ¡Quál lidia bien! governs the whole roll-call down to v. 741: one verb, nine knights. exorado = dorado, 'gilded' (Latin exauratus). lidiador, 'fighter' (lidiar, 'to do battle'). Ruy Diaz is printed here in roman, with no accent, where elsewhere Pidal prints R[o]y Díaz; the text keeps his print. Numbering: the line number 734b is provisional and the letter b is ours. In Pidal's margin the label 730 stands one line high, beside v. 729 (his own footnotes fix 728 on the desmanchar line and 731 on the Mafómat line), and six printed lines run from there to the label 735, so one number too few is available; the second line of this pair is therefore given 734b until the count is settled.

sentences.t:
Minaya Álbar Fáñez, que Çorita mandó,
Martín Antolínez, el Burgalés de pro,
Muño Gustioz, que so criado f[o],
sentences.l:
Minaya Álbar Fáñez, who Çorita commanded,
Martín Antolínez, the Burgalés of worth,
Muño Gustioz, who his fosterling was,
sentences.i: Minaya Álvar Fáñez, who held Zorita, Martín Antolínez, the worthy man of Burgos, Muño Gustioz, who was raised in his household,
sentences.n: que Çorita mandó, 'who governed Zorita'; Pidal refers to his introduction for 'Minaya de Çorita', where he notes that Álvar Fáñez appears as lord of Zorita in documents of 1097 and 1107. el Burgalés de pro, 'the man of Burgos, of worth' (de pro, 'excellent'): Martín Antolínez, who supplied the Çid at Burgos. criado: Pidal, 'criado por el Cid', brought up by the Çid, a fosterling of his house (he compares v. 2902 and his introduction; the modern sense 'servant' does not apply). so = su; f[o] = fue, 'was' (the o is Pidal's).

sentences.t:
Martin Muñoz, el que mandó a Mont Mayor,
Álbar Albar[oz] e Álbar Salvadórez,
Galín Garcia[z], el bueno de Aragón,
Félez Muñoz so sobrino del Campeador!
sentences.l:
Martin Muñoz, he who commanded at Mont Mayor,
Álbar Albar[oz] and Álbar Salvadórez,
Galín Garcia[z], the good-one of Aragón,
Félez Muñoz his nephew of-the Campeador!
sentences.i: Martín Muñoz, who held command at Montemayor, Álvar Álvarez and Álvar Salvadórez, Galín García, the good man from Aragon, and Félez Muñoz, the Campeador's nephew!
sentences.n: Martin (unaccented here, Martín elsewhere: the print's inconsistency is kept) Muñoz of Montemayor — Pidal refers to his introduction for 'Martín Muñoz de Montemayor', where he identifies the place as the Portuguese town that Martín Muñoz governed for Alfonso VI. Albar[oz], Garcia[z]: the patronymic endings are Pidal's. el bueno de Aragón, 'the good man of Aragon'. so sobrino del Campeador, 'his nephew, the Campeador's' (a possessive doubled by de, a common Old Spanish construction). The exclamation opened at v. 734 closes here.

sentences.t:
Desí adelante, quantos que y son,
acorren la seña e a mio Çid el Campeador.
sentences.l:
From-there forward, as-many as there are,
succour the banner and my Çid the Campeador.
sentences.i: And after them, all who are there come to the aid of the banner and of my Çid the Campeador.
sentences.n: Desí adelante, 'from there on, after these' (desí = des + í, 'there'). quantos que y son, 'as many as are there' (y = allí, 'there'). acorren, 'they come to the aid of' (acorrer, as Per Vermudoz demanded in v. 708): the standard is rescued.

sentences.t:
A Minaya Álbar Fáñez matáronle el cavallo,
bien lo acorren mesnadas de cristianos.
sentences.l:
To Minaya Álbar Fáñez they-killed-him the horse,
well him succour companies of Christians.
sentences.i: Minaya Álvar Fáñez had his horse killed under him; the Christian companies come stoutly to his aid.
sentences.n: Tirada 38 (assonance á-o) — Minaya in danger; the Çid wounds Fáriz (Pidal: Minaya en peligro. — El Cid hiere a Fáriz). Every line now ends in á-o (cavallo, cristianos, mano, dando, braço, campo). matáronle el cavallo, 'they killed him the horse' — the le marks the person affected (killed his horse on him); A Minaya … le, the redundant pronoun again. mesnadas, the lord's companies of armed retainers.

sentences.t:
La lança a quebrada, al espada metió mano,
maguer de pie buenos colpes va dando.
sentences.l:
The lance he-has broken, to-the sword he-put hand,
although on foot good blows he-goes giving.
sentences.i: His lance is broken; he set his hand to his sword, and though on foot he goes on dealing good blows.
sentences.n: a quebrada = ha quebrada, 'has broken' (the h unwritten; the participle agrees with la lança). al espada, el/al before a feminine noun beginning with a vowel (cf. el espada, v. 756). maguer de pie: Pidal, 'aunque estaba a pie', 'although he was on foot'. va dando, ir + gerund, 'goes on giving'. The tenses mix — present perfect, preterite, present — in the usual epic way.

sentences.t:
Víolo mio Çid R[o]y Díaz el Castellano,
acostós a un aguazil que tenié buen cavallo,
diol tal espadada con el so diestro braço,
cortól por la çintura, el medio echó en campo.
sentences.l:
Saw-it my Çid R[o]y Díaz the Castilian,
drew-himself-near to an aguazil who had good horse,
gave-him such sword-stroke with the his right arm,
cut-him through the waist, the half he-threw in field.
sentences.i: My Çid Ruy Díaz, the Castilian, saw it; he drew alongside a Moorish commander who had a good horse, and dealt him such a sword-stroke with his right arm that he cut him through at the waist and flung half of him onto the field.
sentences.n: Víolo, 'saw it' (vio + lo). acostós = acostóse, 'drew alongside' (enclitic se cut to s). aguazil: Pidal, the Arabic al-wazir (modern 'vizier'), which meant 'general', 'minister charged with executing justice', 'governor', etc. tenié = tenía. diol = dio + le, 'gave him'; cortól = cortó + le, 'cut him' — the enclitic squeeze. espadada, 'sword-stroke'. el so diestro braço, article + possessive. Pidal's note on v. 751: the Çid likewise cleaves Búcar 'from the helmet to the waist' later on; such strokes, he says, are not incredible given the breadth and weight of the swords of the day, and the chroniclers of the Crusades tell of Godfrey of Bouillon splitting a Muslim from the head to the saddle and cutting another clean in two.

sentences.t:
A Minaya Álbar Fáñez ival dar el cavallo:
“Cavalgad, Minaya, vos sodes el mio diestro braço!
sentences.l:
To Minaya Álbar Fáñez he-went-him to-give the horse:
“Mount, Minaya, you are the my right arm!
sentences.i: He went to give the horse to Minaya Álvar Fáñez: “Mount, Minaya — you are my right arm!
sentences.n: ival = ívale, 'was going to give him' (iva + le; the le, doubling A Minaya, belongs with dar; iva + bare infinitive); the same form is printed íval, with its accent, at v. 776. Cavalgad, 'mount' (imperative). sodes = sois. el mio diestro braço, 'my right arm', echoing the right arm that has just won the horse (v. 750).

sentences.i: This very day I shall have great support from you: the Moors stand firm, they are not yet leaving the field; we must fall on them again.”
sentences.n: abré = habré, 'I shall have' (aver). bando: Pidal, 'auxilio, apoyo', 'help, support' — an abstract sense, he explains, that grows naturally out of the concrete one, the 'party' or body of kinsmen and followers who in the Middle Ages were bound to back one another in claims, feuds and vengeance. firme' son: Pidal, 'firmes están', 'they stand firm' (firme' = firmes with the s dropped before the s of son); aun nos' van: Pidal, 'no se van', 'they are not going' (nos' = non se). Line 755b is wholly in italics in Pidal's print: the whole verse is his restoration, not the manuscript's, and is printed here in plain type; it has no number of its own in his margin, and the letter b is ours. a menester, 'there is need' (aver menester); cometer, 'to attack' (= acometer); de cabo, 'anew, once more'.

sentences.t:
Cavalgó Minaya, el espada en la mano,
por estas fuerças fuerte mientre lidiando,
a los que alcança valos delibrando.
sentences.l:
Mounted Minaya, the sword in the hand,
through these forces strongly fighting,
those whom he-overtakes he-goes-them dispatching.
sentences.i: Minaya mounted, sword in hand, and fought mightily through these hosts, dispatching every man he overtakes.
sentences.n: el espada, 'the sword' (el before a feminine noun beginning with a vowel). fuerças, 'armed forces, hosts'. fuerte mientre = fuertemente, 'strongly': the adverb is still two words, the adjective and mientre (Latin mente). lidiando, a gerund doing duty for a finite verb. a los que alcança, 'those he catches up with'. valos delibrando = los va delibrando: Pidal, delibrar 'despachar, matar', 'to dispatch, kill', and he cites the Libro de Alexandre (488): 'Assi los delivrava cuemo lobo corderos', 'he dispatched them as a wolf does lambs'.

sentences.t:
Mio Çid R[o]y Díaz, el que en buen[a] nasco,
al rey Fáriz tres colpes le avié dado;
sentences.l:
My Çid R[o]y Díaz, he who in good was-born,
to-the king Fáriz three blows to-him had given;
sentences.i: My Çid Ruy Díaz, he who was born in a good hour, had dealt King Fáriz three blows;
sentences.n: el que en buen[a] nasco, the formula once more, here with ora left unsaid: 'he who was born in a good [hour]'; the final a of buen[a], agreeing with the understood ora, is Pidal's. nasco, old strong preterite of nacer. avié dado, 'had given' (avié = había).

sentences.i: two of them missed him, but the third has caught him: down over his hauberk runs the blood; he turned his rein to flee from him off the field.
sentences.n: fallen, from fallir, 'to fail, miss' (present tense in the middle of past narration). el únol ha tomado, 'the one has caught him' (uno + le: únol, the enclitic squeeze); tomar, of a blow, 'to take, catch'. ayuso, 'downward' (ayuso/suso, 'down/up'). destella[n]do, 'dripping, trickling' (Latin destillare) (the n is Pidal's). bolvió la rienda, 'turned the rein', i.e. wheeled his horse away. írsele = irse + le, 'to get away from him'.

sentences.t: Por aquel colpe rancado es el fonssado.
sentences.l: By that blow routed is the army.
sentences.i: By that blow the army is routed.
sentences.n: rancado = arrancado; Pidal glosses rancar el fonssado 'vencer al ejército', 'to defeat the army', and notes that the commoner phrase is arrancar la batalla (vv. 793, 814) or arrancar la lid (vv. 1656, 1819). fonssado, 'army, host'. The king's wound decides the day.

sentences.t:
Martín Antolínez un colpe dio a Galve,
las carbonclas del yelmo echógelas aparte,
cortól el yelmo, que llegó a la carne;
sabet, el otro non gel osó esperar.
sentences.l:
Martín Antolínez a blow gave to Galve,
the carbuncles of-the helmet he-cast-from-him-them aside,
cut-him the helmet, which reached to the flesh;
know-ye, the other not to-him-it dared await.
sentences.i: Martín Antolínez dealt Galve a blow that struck the carbuncles off his helmet and cut through the helmet so that it reached the flesh; and know this, the other did not dare wait for a second.
sentences.n: Tirada 39 (assonance á) — Galve wounded and the Moors routed (Pidal: Galve herido y los moros derrotados). Back to stressed á (esperar, cristiandad, part, alcaz, allá, va, segudar); Galve, aparte and carne (and Galve again in v. 769) end in á-e, the paragogic -e being admitted in the á tirada as in tiradas 32 and 36. carbonclas: Pidal, 'carbuncles' or rubies that adorned the helmet. echógelas = echó + ge + las, 'he struck them off him' (ge = le, as in gelo); cortól = cortó + le. que llegó a la carne, 'which reached the flesh' — the blow, or the cut. sabet, 'know ye', the minstrel's aside. non gel osó esperar, 'did not dare wait for it from him' (gel = ge + lo, the lo probably another blow): Galve, el otro, turns and flees.

sentences.i: Routed are King Fáriz and Galve. Such a good day for Christendom, for the Moors are fleeing on every side!
sentences.n: Arrancado es, singular verb and participle with a double subject, normal in Old Spanish when the verb comes first. ca, 'for'. della [e della] part: Pidal, 'de una y de otra parte', 'on this side and that', as in vv. 2079 and 3139 (or della part e della, v. 1965); the second [e della] is in italics in his print, a restoration. part = parte, cut.

sentences.t:
Los de mio Çid firiendo en alcaz,
el rey Fáriz en Ter[rer] se f[o] entrar,
e a Galve nol cogieron allá;
para Cataluyu[t]h quanto puede se va.
sentences.l:
Those of my Çid striking in pursuit,
the king Fáriz in Ter[rer] himself went to-enter,
and to Galve not-him they-received there;
toward Cataluyu[t]h as-much-as he-can himself goes.
sentences.i: While my Çid's men pressed the pursuit, striking as they went, King Fáriz got into Terrer; but Galve they would not take in there, and he makes off for Calatayud as fast as he can.
sentences.n: Los de mio Çid firiendo, a gerund phrase without a main verb: 'my Çid's men (being) striking'. alcaz: Pidal, the commonest form in the poem (vv. 776, 786, 1147 etc.) beside alcança and alcanço, for modern 'alcance', the pursuit of a fleeing enemy. se f[o] entrar, 'went in' (fo = fue, the o Pidal's; ir + bare infinitive). Ter[rer], Terrer, the last syllable Pidal's as before. nol cogieron, 'they did not take him in' (non + le), presumably the townsmen of Terrer, who shut him out. Cataluyu[t]h: so printed here, with the syllables transposed, beside Calatayu[t]h in v. 777 — the same town, Calatayud; the t in both is Pidal's. quanto puede, 'as fast as he can'.

sentences.t:
El Campeador íval en alcaz,
fata Calatayu[t]h duró el segudar.
sentences.l:
The Campeador went-after-him in pursuit,
as-far-as Calatayu[t]h lasted the chasing.
sentences.i: The Campeador went after him in pursuit; all the way to Calatayud the chase went on.
sentences.n: íval = ívale, 'went after him' (iva + le); compare ival at v. 752, printed without the accent. fata = hasta. segudar: Pidal, 'perseguir', 'to pursue', here used as a noun, 'pursuit' (el segudar). The rout ends at the walls of Calatayud, the town that grieved at the Çid's taking of Alcocer (v. 626).
